back:
Headline: a function template is a recipe, not a function. Each distinct set of template arguments (deduced or explicit) makes the compiler instantiate a separate ordinary function, type-checked for those types, at compile time. Here maxof yields maxof<int> and maxof<double>.
Output:
7
2.5
3
The third printed line uses an explicit argument: maxof<double>(3, 2.5) converts 3 to double, so deduction is skipped.
Interview trap: the body is checked against the actual types at instantiation, so a bug on a path never called with a given type stays silent. Names that do not depend on T (for example a misspelt function name) are still rejected at definition time.

Headline: template argument deduction fails. Both parameters are the same T, and the compiler gets int from 1 and double from 2.0. Deduction does not apply the int-to-double conversion, so there is no viable candidate.
g++ 13 output (key lines):
s02.cpp:9:23: error: no matching function for call to ‘maxof(int, double)’
s02.cpp:9:23: note:   deduced conflicting types for parameter ‘T’ (‘int’ and ‘double’)
Fixes: an explicit argument, maxof<double>(1, 2.0), or two template parameters with std::common_type_t<A, B> as the return type.
Interview trap: the deduction failure is in the call, not in the template definition, and the diagnostic is long. Look for the note line that says deduced conflicting types.

Headline: for a by-value parameter T drops top-level const and reference qualifiers. For T& the const is kept, because it is part of the referred-to type.
Output:
by_value: T=non-pointer
by_ref:   T=const non-pointer
by_value: T=pointer
by_ref:   T=non-pointer
by_value(c): T is int. by_ref(c): T is const int. by_value(arr): the array decays to int*, so T is a pointer. by_ref(arr): T is int[3], an array, not a pointer.
Interview trap: auto x = c; and auto& x = c; follow the same rules as these templates.

front: Template argument deduction for a by-value parameter {{c1::drops top-level const and reference qualifiers}} from the argument type. An array argument passed to a by-value parameter {{c2::decays to a pointer}}. Deduction never uses the {{c3::return type}} of the function.
back: Example: template<class T> void f(T); called as f(c) with const int c gives T=int. The same call to template<class T> void g(T&) gives T=const int. The return type is not part of the deduction; it is checked only after the arguments have fixed T.

Headline: T&& is a forwarding reference only when T is deduced. For an lvalue a, T=int& and the reference collapses to int&. For 42, T=int and x is int&&.
Output:
lvalue
rvalue
std::forward<T>(x) casts x back to the value category it came in with: an lvalue when T is an lvalue reference, an rvalue otherwise. It is a cast, not a move.
Interview trap: x is a named variable, so it is an lvalue inside relay whatever its declared type. Without std::forward the rvalue overload is never chosen (next card).

Headline: lvalue twice. Inside relay the name x is an lvalue, so sink(x) always selects sink(int&), even when the caller passed 42.
Output:
lvalue
lvalue
Fix: sink(std::forward<T>(x)).
Interview trap: T&& is a forwarding reference only for a deduced T of that function. std::vector<T>&& is an ordinary rvalue reference, and forwarding does not apply to it in the same way.

Headline: a full specialization of a function template does not add an overload. It replaces the body for one set of template arguments, and the normal overload rules still apply to the other candidates.
Output:
explicit specialization for int
non-template overload for double
generic template
show(1): T=int, so the specialization is used. show(2.0): the template with T=double and the non-template overload both match exactly, and a non-template wins the tie. show(1.5f): the template matches exactly with T=float, while the non-template needs a float-to-double promotion, so the template wins.
Interview trap: prefer an overload to a full specialization of a function template. Specializations are easy to misplace, and they are invisible to overload resolution.

Headline: the partial specialization is_ptr<T*> matches an unqualified pointer type. The top-level const in int* const makes it a different type, so it falls back to the primary template.
Output:
0
1
0
1
Line 3 (int* const) prints 0. Line 4 (const int*, a pointer to a const int) prints 1, because it matches T* with T=const int.
Interview trap: the standard std::is_pointer handles cv-qualified pointers. A hand-written trait does not, unless you strip cv first with std::remove_cv_t (on this build std::is_pointer_v<int* const> is true).

front: Function templates cannot be {{c1::partially specialized}}; class templates can. To get partial-specialization behaviour for a function, forward to a {{c2::class template}} and specialize that, or use {{c3::overloading}}.
back: Full specializations of function templates are also discouraged, because they do not take part in overload resolution (see the explicit-specialization card). The forwarding pattern is the standard way to write a constrained, partially specialized implementation.

front: Implement my_remove_const<T> and its alias my_remove_const_t<T> with partial specialization. Show it on const int, int, const int* and int* const, and predict the output.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <type_traits>

template <typename T>
struct my_remove_const { using type = T; };

template <typename T>
struct my_remove_const<const T> { using type = T; };

template <typename T>
using my_remove_const_t = typename my_remove_const<T>::type;

int main() {
    std::cout << std::is_same_v<my_remove_const_t<const int>, int> << '\n';
    std::cout << std::is_same_v<my_remove_const_t<int>, int> << '\n';
    std::cout << std::is_same_v<my_remove_const_t<const int*>, const int*> << '\n';
    std::cout << std::is_same_v<my_remove_const_t<int* const>, int*> << '\n';
}
Output:
1
1
1
1
Headline: the partial specialization my_remove_const<const T> strips one top-level const. const int* is a non-const pointer to a const int, so nothing is stripped. int* const matches const T with T=int*.
Interview trap: the standard version is std::remove_const. The follow-up is volatile: std::remove_cv strips both, and std::remove_cvref also strips the reference.

Headline: std::vector<bool> is an explicit specialization of std::vector that packs bits. Its operator[] returns a proxy object, std::vector<bool>::reference, by value, so the address-of operator has nothing to take.
g++ 13 output (key lines):
s11.cpp:6:23: error: taking address of rvalue [-fpermissive]
s11.cpp:6:15: error: cannot convert ‘std::vector<bool>::reference*’ to ‘bool*’ in initialization
Fix: use std::vector<char> or std::vector<std::uint8_t>, or keep the value and do not take a pointer to it.
Interview trap: auto r = flags[0]; copies the proxy, not the bool, so later writes to the vector change r. Code that is generic over T hits this specialization silently.

Headline: SFINAE removes a candidate when substituting the template arguments into its signature fails. std::enable_if_t<false, int> has no type, so that candidate disappears and the other one is chosen. The two enable_if conditions differ, so the two templates have different template-parameter lists and are distinct overloads.
Output:
integral 7
floating 2.500000
Interview trap: SFINAE only applies to errors in the immediate context of the signature. An error inside the function body after substitution is a hard error that stops compilation, not a removed candidate.

Headline: template<std::integral T> is shorthand for a requires-clause. A candidate whose constraint fails is removed from the overload set during overload resolution, the same effect as SFINAE, but the constraint is written once and named in the diagnostic.
Output:
42
10
Interview trap: when two overloads both match, the more constrained one wins (subsumption). A constraint can only test what its expression says; it does not check the semantics of the function.

Headline: the constraint integral<double> is false, so the candidate is not viable.
Key lines of g++ 13 output:
s14.cpp:8:23: error: no matching function for call to ‘twice(double)’
s14.cpp:5:3: note: constraints not satisfied
Fix: change the constraint (for example std::floating_point) or add an overload, and do not call twice with a double.
Interview trap: with std::enable_if you get a message about a missing ::type in a default argument, which is much harder to read. The concept version names the failing predicate directly.

front: A failed constraint removes that template from the overload set during {{c1::overload resolution}}, and the call is an error only when {{c2::no candidate}} remains. The resulting diagnostic names the {{c3::unsatisfied constraint}}.
back: This is the same mechanism as SFINAE, but the concept version fails at the call with the constraint named, instead of with a substitution error inside a default argument.

Headline: the requires expression checks that x.price() is valid and that its result converts to double. It checks the declaration only, not the value.
Output:
199
0
Interview trap: a concept cannot tell that price() returns something sensible. Semantic requirements (for example a positive price) still need unit tests.

front: Trade-off: in a C++ pricing library, when do you constrain a template with SFINAE (std::enable_if) and when with C++20 concepts? Give the reasons and one case where SFINAE is still the right tool.
back:
Concepts: the constraint is written once and read in the signature. Overloads are ranked by subsumption, and diagnostics name the failing predicate. Use them for all new C++20 code.
SFINAE: still needed for code that must compile as C++17, and for trait classes that test a member with a std::void_t-style detection idiom, where a class template partial specialization is the cleanest form.
Interview trap: a concept checks only what its requires expression states. Do not conclude a type is correct because it satisfies a concept.

Headline: sizeof...(Ts) is the pack length, known at compile time. (xs + ... + 0) is a binary right fold: it expands to xs1 + (xs2 + (... + 0)).
Output:
3
6
3.75
The return type of sum(1.5, 2.25) is double because the elements are double. sum() with no argument returns the initial int 0.
Interview trap: the return type is deduced from the arguments, so sum() and sum(1.5) return different types. An explicit return type removes that surprise.
Python vs C++: Python's *args is a runtime tuple. A C++ pack is expanded at compile time, so no container exists unless you store one (for example in std::tuple).

Headline: a unary fold over + of an empty pack has no value. Only && (true), || (false) and the comma operator (void()) have a defined value for an empty pack.
g++ 13 output:
s19.cpp:4:35: error: fold of empty expansion over operator+
Fix: a binary fold with an initial value, (xs + ... + 0).
Interview trap: the template definition is accepted, and the error appears only when sum<> is instantiated with an empty pack.

front: For an empty parameter pack, the unary fold (... && args) gives {{c1::true}}, (... || args) gives {{c2::false}}, and the comma fold gives {{c3::void()}}. For any other operator you need a binary fold with an {{c4::initial value}}.
back: This is why sum() with (xs + ...) is ill-formed, and (xs + ... + 0) compiles.

Headline: the comma fold ((cout << ' ' << tail), ...) applies the expression to each tail element in order. The second call passes an empty tail, which is valid: the comma fold of an empty pack is void(), so only the head is printed.
Output:
1 2.5 abc
done
Interview trap: a user-defined type can overload the comma operator, and that changes what the fold does. Wrapping each operand in static_cast<void>(...) makes the fold use the built-in comma.

Headline: Instrument<Derived> calls pv_impl on the derived type through a static cast of this. The call is bound at compile time, so there is no vtable and the compiler can inline it.
Output:
95.2381
50
Bond: 100/1.05, the PV of one cash flow of 100 one year out at 5%, is 95.2381. Swap here is a toy formula, 1000 times the rate.
Interview trap: Instrument<Bond> and Instrument<Swap> are unrelated types, so you cannot keep them together in one std::vector of a common base. That is the cost of static dispatch.

front: Trade-off: virtual functions against CRTP for pricing kernels. What does each cost, and which would you use for the innermost Monte Carlo loop and for a book of heterogeneous trades? Python-vs-C++: how does this differ from Python method dispatch?
back:
Virtual: one indirect call through a vtable pointer stored in each object. The compiler usually cannot inline across it, and objects are larger. It is the right tool for a heterogeneous book: a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Trade>> that dispatches once per trade.
CRTP: zero-overhead, inlinable, each derived type is a separate instantiation. It is the right tool for the innermost loop, where the product type is fixed at compile time.
Python: every method call is a runtime lookup on the object. C++ virtual calls are cheaper, and CRTP removes the call entirely.
Interview trap: "virtual is slow" is an overstatement. In a pricing loop the cost is usually the lost inlining and worse memory layout, so measure before choosing.

Headline: Bond names Swap as its CRTP argument. The base casts this (a Bond) to Swap*, and Swap::pv_impl runs on a Bond object. Nothing in the compiler flags this.
Output (undefined behaviour, do not rely on it):
50
The correct value is 95.2381, and Bond::pv_impl never runs. Under -Wall -Wextra -O2 g++ 13 gives no diagnostic.
Fix: struct Bond : Instrument<Bond>. To catch this at compile time, add a namespace-scope check after the definition: static_assert(std::is_base_of_v<Instrument<Bond>, Bond>, "CRTP argument must name this class");. With that check in place, g++ 13 reports (key line):
error: static assertion failed: CRTP argument must name this class
Interview trap: a static_assert inside Bond does not work, because Bond is incomplete there. Place the check after the class.

Headline: Counted<Bond> and Counted<Swap> are different classes, so each has its own static inline member live. The copy constructor is needed so that copies are counted too.
Output:
live bonds inside scope: 3
live bonds: 2, live swaps: 1
Interview trap: the counter is not thread-safe. Use std::atomic<int> if instances are created on several threads.

Headline: constexpr means the function can be evaluated at compile time, not that it is. The static_assert and the constexpr local force compile-time evaluation. Calling the same function with a runtime n runs it at runtime.
Output:
3628800
479001600
Interview trap: a constexpr function that is called with a runtime value is an ordinary function, so nothing warns you that it ran at runtime. Use consteval (next card) when compile time is the requirement.

Headline: consteval makes a function an immediate function: every call must be a constant expression. n is a runtime variable, so the call is rejected.
g++ 13 output (key lines):
s27.cpp:11:23: error: the value of ‘n’ is not usable in a constant expression
s27.cpp:10:9: note: ‘int n’ is not const
Fix: make n constexpr, or drop consteval and let the function run at runtime.
Interview trap: use consteval for compile-time-only helpers, such as table builders. With constexpr the same mistake compiles silently and runs at runtime.

Headline: a constexpr variable must hold a constant. A std::vector allocates memory with operator new, which C++20 allows only for transient allocation inside a constant evaluation that is freed before it ends.
g++ 13 output (key line):
/usr/include/c++/13/bits/allocator.h:195:52: error: ‘std::vector<double>(std::initializer_list<double>{((const double*)(& const double [2]{1.0e+0, 9.4999999999999996e-1})), 2}, std::allocator<double>())’ is not a constant expression because it refers to a result of ‘operator new’
Fix: std::array, as in the table card. Note that libstdc++ accepts constexpr double e = std::exp(1.0); and std::pow as an extension, but the C++20 standard does not guarantee them to be constexpr, so do not rely on this for portable code.
Interview trap: a constexpr container is only possible in C++20 if its memory is freed within the same constant evaluation.

front: A constexpr function {{c1::may}} be evaluated at compile time. Every call to a consteval function {{c2::must}} be a constant expression. A constinit variable with static storage is {{c3::constant-initialized}}, but it is {{c4::not necessarily const}}.
back: constinit removes the static-initialization-order problem for globals without making them read-only. Use it for a global that must be initialized at compile time and can change at runtime.

Headline: the table is computed by multiplication, not by std::pow, which the C++20 standard does not guarantee to be constexpr. Each entry is \(1/(1+r)^t\), and the array sits in constant storage with no runtime cost.
Output:
1
0.952381
0.907029
0.863838
0.822702
0.783526
Check: \(1/1.05 = 0.952381\), \(1/1.05^2 = 0.907029\), \(1/1.05^5 = 0.783526\).
Interview trap: a large compile-time table costs compile time and binary size. Use constexpr for small fixed tables, and a runtime loop for curve-dependent tables.

Headline: std::decay_t turns arrays into pointers, removes references, and removes cv-qualifiers. std::remove_cvref_t removes cv and references but not array-ness. std::remove_const_t acts on the pointer itself, not on the pointee.
Output:
1
1
1
0
1
Line 4: const int* is a non-const pointer to a const int, so remove_const leaves it unchanged. Line 5: const int* const loses its top-level const and becomes const int*.
Interview trap: the usual bug is a const on the pointee being read as a const on the pointer. Read the declaration from right to left.

Headline: the partial specialization's arguments are decltype expressions. If any of them fails to substitute, the specialization is removed and the primary template (false) applies.
Output:
1
0
0
Interview trap: older compilers did not handle the naive void_t alias correctly (CWG 1558). The standard std::void_t works on current compilers. In C++20 a requires expression or a concept is the cleaner form of the same test.

Headline: if constexpr inside a template discards the branch whose condition is false, and a discarded branch is not instantiated. For int, x.name() is never checked.
Output:
integer 42
instrument UKT 4.25 2034
Interview trap: with a plain if the same program fails to compile for int, because both branches are instantiated. if constexpr only discards inside a template, and only when the condition depends on a template parameter.

Headline: Model and Payoff are compile-time policies. Each Pricer<Model,Payoff> is a separate type with direct, inlinable calls. In Python the strategy is a runtime object looked up by name each time.
Output:
2.89692
24.5988
Scenario z=0: \(S_T = 100e^{0.03} = 103.045\), payoff 3.045, times \(e^{-0.05}=0.951229\), gives 2.8969. Scenario z=1: \(S_T = 125.860\), payoff 25.860, price 24.599. This is one scenario, not an expectation; a real Monte Carlo averages over many z.
Interview trap: the policy interface is implicit. A missing method is reported inside Pricer's body at the point of use, not where the policy is declared. A concept on each policy gives a clear error at the declaration.

Headline: an empty class takes at least one byte. As an empty base, the compiler can overlap it with the first member (empty base optimisation), so WithBase is 8 bytes. As a member it takes its own byte and padding, so WithMember is 16.
Output:
sizeof(Empty)      = 1
sizeof(WithBase)   = 8
sizeof(WithMember) = 16
Interview trap: [[no_unique_address]] (C++20) gives the member form the same saving, but support depends on the compiler. Stateless policies should be empty bases or use this attribute.

front: Policies chosen as template parameters are fixed at {{c1::compile time}}, so the policy calls are {{c2::inlined}} in the generated code. A stateless policy used as a base class takes {{c3::zero bytes}} through {{c4::empty base optimisation}}.
back: Each distinct combination of policies is a separate instantiation, so the cost is code size and compile time, not runtime dispatch.

Headline: std::function is a type-erased wrapper. Here the lambda captures one double, so it is 8 bytes, and the wrapper is 32 bytes on this build (libstdc++, g++ 13). Calls through it are indirect and cannot be inlined.
Output:
sizeof(lambda)        = 8
sizeof(std::function) = 32
f(4) = 2
lam(4) = 2
Interview trap: the 32 is a library detail, not a rule. Captures above the implementation's small-buffer size go to the heap, so a big lambda passed through std::function into a hot loop can cost allocations as well as indirection.

front: Trade-off: a numerical integrator that is called with a payoff in an inner Monte Carlo loop. Compare taking the payoff as a template parameter F with taking it as std::function<double(double)>. Which do you choose, and when is the other one better?
back:
Template parameter: every distinct lambda gets its own instantiation, so the call inlines into the loop. The cost is code size and compile time per callable type.
std::function: one instantiation serves every callable with that signature. It can be stored in a container, a class member or a configuration, and chosen at runtime from a trade blotter, at the cost of an indirect call per evaluation and possible heap allocation.
Interview trap: the indirect call is often small next to the work in the loop body. Profile first, because the real loss is usually the blocked inlining in the innermost loop.

front: Python vs C++: a Python function def price(inst): return inst.pv() and the C++ template template<class I> double price(const I& i) { return i.pv(); }. When does each one fail, and what does the failure look like?
back:
Python: a missing method fails at runtime, on the call that reaches it, with an AttributeError.
C++ template: the function is checked per instantiation. A missing pv fails at compile time at the call site, and the diagnostic names the missing member. There are no runtime type errors, but the message can be long: a concept on I states the requirement once and gives a clean error.
Interview trap: a template is not a function that accepts all types. Its body is checked only for the types you instantiate, so an unused path can hide an error until something uses it.

Headline: main.cpp cannot see the definition, so it cannot instantiate sq<int>. sq.cpp never instantiates it either, so no object file defines the symbol and the link fails.
Linker output (key line):
s40_main.cpp:(.text.startup+0x1e): undefined reference to `int sq<int>(int)'
Fix 1 (usual): put the definition in the header, so every translation unit can instantiate it. Fix 2: keep the definition in sq.cpp and add an explicit instantiation template int sq<int>(int);. With the explicit instantiation the two-file program links and prints 9 (verified with g++ 13).
Interview trap: an explicit instantiation covers only the types you list. Header definitions cost compile time in every translation unit, and extern template declarations in the header, with one explicit instantiation in a .cpp, avoid repeated instantiation in every translation unit.
